overview: This record covers medieval Denmark in 1100-1400, a Christian kingdom of farms, towns, landowners and churches. Its rulers also held territories beyond modern Denmark. The later Kalmar Union did not erase Denmark, and the map's 1400 boundary is not the end of the kingdom.

periods.title: Churches, towns and royal government
periods.summary: New building techniques and urban trades developed within an agricultural society.

periods.title: Written law and Baltic connections
periods.summary: The Law of Jutland was issued in 1241. Denmark's Estonian possessions were sold in 1346.

periods.title: Beginning of the Kalmar Union
periods.summary: Denmark joined Norway and Sweden under a shared monarch; the kingdoms retained distinct histories.

items.text: Excavations at Thomas B. Thriges Gade in Odense uncovered part of a brick house from the early 1200s. Brick was still an expensive material, so the building suggests a wealthy household. It is not a model for every Danish home.

From the 1300s, some Odense backyards had barrel-shaped latrine installations. Archaeology reveals planned places for waste within increasingly crowded plots. A town needed maintenance and disposal systems as well as churches and markets.

One latrine preserved wooden bowls and two carefully shaped sticks. The excavator suggests a wiping arrangement using cloth or leather and water. This is an interpretation of particular finds, not proof that medieval Denmark had one standard toilet kit.

Odense's backyards also held animals and garden plots. Bone finds record meat consumption, while written sources mention cabbage and apple gardens. Town residents could combine craft or commerce with producing some food.

Roskilde Cathedral was built in brick during the 1100s and 1200s. Its Gothic design helped spread brick church architecture through northern Europe. Turning clay into durable, repeated building units supported ambitious construction.

The cathedral accumulated porches, chapels and alterations over later centuries. A visitor's view is therefore a sequence of building projects. Its later royal tombs should not all be imagined inside the earliest medieval church.

The National Museum preserves imagery of the golden altar frontal from Lisbjerg Church, dated 1135. Mary and the child occupy its religious programme. A richly decorated altar focused attention during worship; it was not ordinary household furniture.

Medieval Danish landowners, townspeople and church institutions used objects and images to express status. The museum distinguishes these settings. A costly surviving church object reveals a patron's priorities more readily than the daily possessions of a poor family.

sections.title: Law and a wider political world

items.text: Valdemar II issued the Law of Jutland at Vordingborg in 1241 with the participation of leading royal and church figures. Writing law made rules easier to preserve and consult, although possessing a law book did not guarantee equal treatment in every dispute.

Mæth logh skall land bygges means “With law shall the land be built.” This Danish opening survives in Lund manuscript 25 of the Law of Jutland. That particular copy dates to the 1400s-1500s, later than the 1241 law and this map segment; its spelling is not modern Danish.

Danish rule included northern Estonian territory, explaining Baltic features in some atlas snapshots. The 1346 sale to the Teutonic Order changed sovereignty. A distant possession should not be treated as evidence that its inhabitants became culturally identical to people in Jutland.

In 1397 Erik was crowned over Denmark, Norway and Sweden in the union associated with Queen Margrete. Sharing a monarch joined political interests without turning the three kingdoms into one uniform community.

ending.text: Denmark continued beyond 1400 within the changing Kalmar Union. The union was a political arrangement among kingdoms, not the disappearance of Danish society. Later divisions and religious changes belong to subsequent phases; this medieval atlas segment has no single national fall date.
